lines.text: Investigators, journalists, lawyers and researchers share one problem.
Too much evidence to read, and a result nobody can later prove was not changed.
Sealbook is an app for exactly that. It works in three steps.
You bring the material in. The app reads all of it and proposes connections, each shown with the exact place it came from.
A person approves or declines each one with a signature, and the record is sealed, so anyone can check it later.
Four invented cases show how that helps.
One: a freight company pays a supplier, a consultant, a guarantor and a ship agent. Four desks, four clean files.
Are these four people, or one man under four names?
Kassar. Qassar. Khassar. Kasar. And on one licence, the name in Arabic.
Four spellings, two alphabets, one man. And one who is not him: a surveyor with the same name, born elsewhere.
The app proposed these links, each with the passage behind it. Fixed rules with no AI model found 4 of the 6 true links, enough to join all his records.
A person declines the surveyor, and signs each decision with a passkey, a key on their own device.
The case closes on a conclusion, signed by a person and checked by a colleague: one man, on four desks, under four names.
Two: a workshop burns down at night. The bookkeeper says she spent the evening at her sister's house, 34 kilometres away.
Was she? There are 41 statements to read.
The app flags that two exhibit sheets made from her own phone place her at the workshop that same day.
A person reads the times, 21:52 and 22:07, and concludes she was there.
Three: a flood video spreads as breaking news.
Is it new? The tip line holds 36 clips that look alike.
The app compares their sound and ties the viral clip to a video posted two years earlier. It had been cropped and mirrored, so the picture no longer matched.
8 of 9 reposts were tied this way. One muted copy is missed. A person signs that the clip is old.
Four: a nurse boards a night bus and is never seen again.
Where do you look? The bus company's logs run to several hundred lines.
A supervisor's statement says when the driver was last seen. From that night, the app finds 73 days in which no log names him.
A person records it as a lead to follow, not a finding.
Every decision is signed by a person. A court can check the sealed package offline; here, on a test package.
The machine reads more than a person can, and finds the links. A person approves every one.
